correctness.rationale: For odd m,n>=3, opposite initial part majorities cause only L's initial red and R's initial blue vertices to move their opinions until the first group tips. Their distinct first-selection order is a uniform permutation; L flips first iff among the first a+b-1 relevant activations at least a are from the r=x L-red vertices, giving exactly the hypergeometric tail H. Once part majorities agree, all further updates reinforce them, and every vertex is almost surely eventually updated; initial part-majority agreement is already monotone. Binomial initial counts and color exchange give the stated unconditional R excluding initial global ties. With m/n->rho in [1,infinity), independent unit-rate first-activation order statistics concentrate around |X|/m, |Y|/n for CLT margins; the inversion wedge XY<0, |Y|<|X|<rho |Y| has Gaussian probability (1/pi)arcsin((rho-1)/(rho+1)). Independently recoded an absorbing state recursion and rational hypergeometric first-tip count; tested all 324 conditional count configurations over m,n in {3,5,7}, plus example R_(3,3)=9/160 and other samples. Finite checks do not establish the asymptotic limit.

originality.rationale: The precise complete-bipartite random-sequential strict-majority reversal probability and finite-ratio Gaussian-arcsine limit are not implied by the inspected node-dynamics consensus-time results on complete/dense random graphs, or by signal-revelation majority on sparse random graphs and neighbor-copy voter processes. The public 2018 primary full text explicitly focuses on complete and dense Erdos–Renyi consensus-time estimates, not two odd bipartition groups with exact hypergeometric first-tipping law. Best-of-knowledge originality with possibility of an unindexed two-community majority race identity.
residual_risks: The exact formula excludes even part sizes and globally tied initial profiles by definition.
The arcsine limit requires both parts to diverge and their size ratio to converge to a finite rho>=1; it does not justify diverging-ratio interchanges.

value.rationale: Majority reversals are the central efficiency/fidelity question for social learning; complete bipartite communities are an elementary but nontrivial topology exhibiting opposing group majorities. The exact finite hypergeometric probability and nontrivial arcsine size-imbalance law quantify when almost-sure consensus contradicts the initial global majority. These distinguish convergence from aggregation accuracy, with a sharp 3:1 limiting value 1/6.
